clinicalPearls: OCA1 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in TYR, the gene encoding tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme of melanin synthesis.
It is subdivided into OCA1A, with complete absence of tyrosinase activity and lifelong total lack of melanin, and OCA1B, with residual activity allowing some pigment to accumulate over time.

OCA1A presents with white hair, milky-white skin and translucent blue-grey or pink irides that never darken, whereas OCA1B children may develop light-yellow or blond hair and some skin and iris pigment with age.
The ocular phenotype is obligatory and includes nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, iris transillumination, reduced visual acuity and photophobia.
Misrouting of optic-nerve fibres with excessive decussation at the chiasm disrupts binocular vision and causes strabismus and abnormal visual-evoked potentials.
The temperature-sensitive OCA1B variant can produce darker hair in cooler acral areas and lighter hair in warmer regions, reflecting the thermolability of the mutant enzyme.
Melanin deficiency confers a markedly increased lifetime risk of actinic damage and skin cancer, demanding rigorous photoprotection.
Unlike syndromic albinism such as Hermansky-Pudlak or Chediak-Higashi, OCA1 is non-syndromic without bleeding diathesis or immune defect.
reference.pathophysiology: Oculocutaneous albinism type 1 is an autosomal recessive disorder of melanin biosynthesis caused by pathogenic variants in TYR, which encodes tyrosinase, the copper-dependent enzyme that catalyses the first and rate-limiting steps of melanogenesis: the hydroxylation of tyrosine to dihydroxyphenylalanine and its subsequent oxidation to dopaquinone within melanosomes of skin, hair-bulb and ocular melanocytes and the retinal pigment epithelium. In OCA1A, null variants abolish enzyme activity entirely, so no eumelanin or phaeomelanin is ever produced, giving lifelong complete absence of pigment; in OCA1B, hypomorphic variants leave partial, sometimes temperature-sensitive, residual activity that permits gradual accumulation of some melanin, accounting for the milder and evolving phenotype. Because melanin in the developing eye is essential for normal foveal development and for correct guidance of retinal ganglion-cell axons at the optic chiasm, its absence causes foveal hypoplasia, reduced visual acuity, nystagmus, iris and retinal hypopigmentation with transillumination, and abnormal, excessive crossing of nerve fibres to the contralateral hemisphere that impairs stereopsis. The lack of cutaneous melanin removes protection against ultraviolet radiation, so keratinocytes and melanocytes accumulate photodamage, explaining the high incidence of solar keratoses and both melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer; hearing is unaffected because tyrosinase has no role in cochlear function, distinguishing OCA1 from pigment-related syndromic deafness.
additionalDifferentials: Oculocutaneous albinism types 2, 3 and 4 from OCA2, TYRP1 and SLC45A2 variants
Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome with albinism plus a bleeding tendency and pulmonary fibrosis
Chediak-Higashi syndrome with albinism, immune deficiency and giant granules
Ocular albinism with predominantly ocular hypopigmentation and X-linked inheritance
Griscelli syndrome with silvery hair and immune or neurological features
Waardenburg syndrome with patchy depigmentation and deafness
Phenylketonuria and other causes of generalised skin and hair hypopigmentation
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of TYR with differentiation of OCA1A from OCA1B
Full ophthalmological assessment including acuity, nystagmus and iris transillumination
Optical coherence tomography to demonstrate foveal hypoplasia
Visual-evoked potentials to detect abnormal chiasmal misrouting
Dermatological examination and regular skin-cancer surveillance
Platelet function studies if a Hermansky-Pudlak phenotype is suspected
Family and pedigree evaluation with carrier counselling
redFlags: New, changing or pigmented cutaneous lesion suggesting melanoma or other skin cancer
Extensive actinic damage or non-healing sun-exposed skin lesions
Rapidly worsening or asymmetric nystagmus prompting reassessment for other pathology
Bleeding tendency or recurrent infection suggesting a syndromic albinism rather than OCA1
Severe photophobia limiting function and education in a child
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal provided rigorous photoprotection and skin-cancer surveillance are maintained; visual acuity is permanently reduced and does not normalise, though it is often stable and may be marginally better in OCA1B, and low-vision support enables good functional independence.
pitfalls: Assuming visual acuity will improve with pigment accumulation in OCA1B when foveal hypoplasia is fixed
Neglecting lifelong skin-cancer surveillance and photoprotection counselling
Failing to distinguish non-syndromic OCA1 from Hermansky-Pudlak or Chediak-Higashi with their systemic risks
Mistaking evolving OCA1B pigmentation for a milder OCA2 or for normal variation
Attributing associated deafness to albinism when it points instead to Waardenburg or another diagnosis
